title: Living ashtpadi 14

segments.voice: Yesterday, daataa: one Giver, and every other hand a link in the chain. Today we live the fourteenth ashtpadi, through a story from the janamsakhis.

Two invitations arrive in the same town on the same day. One is from a rich official, Malik Bhago, who is throwing a grand feast and expects every holy man around to attend. The other is from Bhai Lalo, a carpenter, who can offer only plain, coarse bread. Guru Nanak is in town. Everyone assumes he'll go to the feast. He goes to the carpenter's house. And when the insulted official demands to know why, the answer, as Sikhs tell it, becomes a moment in the janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life.
screen: `TWO INVITATIONS, ONE TOWN.` → `A FEAST, OR A CARPENTER'S BREAD.` → `HE GOES TO THE CARPENTER.`

segments.voice: Here's how the story goes. Guru Nanak takes Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a rich cake from Malik Bhago's feast in the other, and squeezes both. From Lalo's bread, the story says, comes milk. From Bhago's, blood. Bhago's wealth had been squeezed out of the poor; Lalo's bread had been earned with his own hands. It's a story, told and retold, not a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs hear it as a picture rather than a lab report. But the picture is exactly what the fourteenth ashtpadi has been saying. Malik Bhago is siaanap made flesh: the clever official, working angles, rich from other people's labor, leaning on power and on people who could be bought. Lalo is the opposite: simple, straight, one hope. Sikhs have a word for Lalo's kind of living: kirat, honest work. Kirat karni, earning by honest labor, is one of three duties Sikh teaching names together, alongside remembering the Name and sharing what you have. It isn't glamorous. It's showing up, doing the job straight, charging a fair price, not cutting the corner when nobody would notice. And see what simplicity buys. Malik Bhago has to keep track of his schemes, his debts, his flatterers. Lalo has nothing to keep track of. His bread is just bread. That's living ashtpadi fourteen: not becoming naive, but choosing, again and again, the way that needs no angles.
screen: `MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.` · `A STORY, HEARD AS A PICTURE.` · `KIRAT: HONEST WORK.` · `NOTHING TO KEEP TRACK OF.` · then, large: `SIMPLE, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of something on your plate this week where there's a shortcut, a little angle, a convenient half-truth, and picture the angled way and how much tracking it would take. Then picture the plain way, the honest email, the fair price, the work done properly, and feel how much lighter it is to carry. Choose it, here, quietly.
Kirat, honest work. Bhai Lalo's plain bread, the simple straight way that needs no angles and leaves nothing to keep track of.
Your line: simple, straight. Plain bread is just bread, with nothing to keep track of. More tomorrow.

chat.says: Why did Guru Nanak pick the carpenter's plain bread over the rich man's feast?
options: In the story, Lalo's bread was honestly earned, kirat, while Bhago's wealth was squeezed from the poor.
Because Sikh teaching says wealth itself is evil, so anyone with money should be avoided.
Because the carpenter was family, and a Guru always eats with relatives before others.
chat.meaning: In the janamsakhi story, milk came from Lalo's bread and blood from Bhago's: honest work, kirat, against wealth squeezed from the poor.
